title: THE STRANGER WHO REFUSED MY $1,000 — 35 YEARS LATER, MY WIFE SAW HIS FACE ON LIVE TELEVISION AND BEGAN TO CRY – MP STORY
excerpt: More than 35 years ago, my wife and I were driving home shortly after 2:15 a.m. when our car suddenly died on a deserted highway.
author: admin

blocks.text: More than 35 years ago, my wife and I were driving home shortly after 2:15 a.m. when our car suddenly died on a deserted highway.

There were no gas stations. No houses. No streetlights. No cell phones. Just miles of darkness stretching in every direction and a freezing wind that seemed to seep through the doors of our old sedan.
We sat there for almost two hours, wondering whether we would have to spend the rest of the night inside that freezing car.
Then a beat-up pickup truck appeared in the distance.
A young college student climbed out, asked if we were safe, and without hesitation drove us 42 miles to the nearest town.
When I tried to give him $1,000 for saving us, he smiled and gently pushed the money back.
“Just promise you’ll help someone else someday,” he said.
For more than three decades, my wife and I remembered that young man as one of the kindest strangers we had ever encountered.
Then, one morning, my wife called me crying.
I reached for the remote, and when the screen lit up, my heart nearly stopped.
The same eyes. The same smile. The same unmistakable face.
The young stranger who once drove two frightened people 42 miles through the darkness had become one of the most famous men in the world.
But what happened next would reveal something about that night that neither my wife nor I could have imagined.
My name is Robert Mitchell. I am 72 years old, and this is the story I have carried in my heart for most of my adult life.
My wife, Margaret, and I had been married for eleven years. We were living in a small town outside Albuquerque, New Mexico, where I worked as a mechanic and Margaret worked as a nurse.
Our house was modest, our car was old, and most months we had to be careful about every dollar we spent.
We had a six-year-old daughter named Emily, who was staying with Margaret’s sister that weekend while we attended a family gathering several hours away.
We left shortly after midnight because I wanted to get home before sunrise.
Margaret had fallen asleep in the passenger seat, wrapped in her coat, while I drove along a nearly empty stretch of highway.
At approximately 2:17 a.m., the headlights flickered.
I guided the car onto the shoulder and tried turning the ignition.
I lifted the hood, even though I knew very little about repairing engines in the dark.
I checked the battery connections, examined the hoses, and tried to find anything obvious.
Our headlights were barely illuminating the road, and there wasn’t another vehicle in sight.
We had no mobile phones. In those days, most ordinary families didn’t carry them.
The nearest telephone could have been miles away.
After twenty minutes, Margaret began getting worried.
“Of course,” I said, trying to sound confident.
Margaret rubbed her hands together and pulled her coat tighter around her shoulders.
Then, just as I was beginning to consider walking toward the nearest town, two headlights appeared in the distance.
It approached slowly before stopping behind our car.
He looked about twenty or twenty-one years old. He wore faded jeans, a brown jacket, and an old university sweatshirt.
One headlight was slightly dimmer than the other. The passenger-side door was scratched, and the engine sounded as though it had been repaired more times than I could count.
“Car died. We’ve been sitting here for nearly two hours.”
“No,” I answered. “We don’t even have a phone.”
Then he said something I have never forgotten.
“All right. Let’s get you somewhere warm.”
I asked whether he could take us to the nearest gas station.
“There’s a small town about forty-two miles from here. There’s a diner and a motel. I’ll take you there.”
Forty-two miles was a long way to ask of a complete stranger.
“You’re not going to leave this lady sitting out here all night, are you?”
Margaret laughed for the first time that evening.
Within minutes, we had locked our belongings inside our car and climbed into his pickup.
The inside was cluttered with textbooks, notebooks, and empty coffee cups.
There was a small photograph tucked above the dashboard.
It showed an elderly woman standing beside a young boy.
I noticed the photograph because the woman had the same gentle eyes as the young man.
For the first few miles, we made ordinary conversation.
He told us he was a college student studying engineering. He worked part-time at a grocery store and sometimes helped a mechanic to earn extra money.
He was attending the University of New Mexico.
I asked whether he was planning to become an engineer.
“Hopefully. Right now, I’m mostly trying to afford tuition.”
Margaret asked whether his family lived nearby.
“My grandmother is back in Oklahoma. She’s the only family I’ve really got.”
He explained that his parents had died when he was young.
His grandmother had raised him despite having very little money.
She worked cleaning houses and sewing clothes for neighbors to make sure he could attend school.
“She always tells me that being poor isn’t an excuse for being unkind,” he said.
